title: Student reportedly loses hand from police grenade amid France's education protests
summary: A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday, a local official said, on ‌the eve of a national demonstration by the pupils' union…

image.caption: Firefighters arrive to extinguish a fire in front of Jean-Louis Cyffle high school in Nancy, France, on Monday, on the sidelines of nationwide protests by high-school students over learning conditions. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday, a local official said, on ‌the eve of a national demonstration by the pupils' union against underfunding, overcrowding and dilapidation.
Security officials concerned about organized protest scheduled for Tuesday in Paris
Up to 500 schools in France to remain closed amid student protests

The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated, in the town of Lens as the wave of school protests entered its third week.
François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact ​circumstances, saying some 200-250 protesters had been hurling objects at police.

Six months out from ​an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron, his government and the far-right National Rally, spearheaded by presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen, have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests, an accusation the LFI denies.
Rights groups accuse police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors including batons, tear gas and other riot-control weapons.

Among several investigations into police methods, authorities ⁠are examining the case of a 16-year-old who suffered an eye injury after ‌police fired rubber bullets into a crowd of protesters, according to his friends.
The LFI, headed by presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, denies encouraging violence and accuses the government of politicizing the issue and neglecting pupils' interests.

The protests have put more pressure on a government trying to narrow a budget deficit as investor concerns about states' finances grow, briefly pushing the yield on France's 10-year bonds to a 24-year ⁠high over five per cent last week and raising the likely cost of future borrowing.
Some 400 to 500 high schools were closed or partially closed as demonstrations and blockades showed no sign of abating ahead of Tuesday's nationwide protest.
The protests began in September in Paris, focusing on the deprived suburbs, before spreading. The government says they ‌have been hijacked and morphed into urban violence.
"Our priority is to restore order," Maud Bregeon, spokesperson for the French government, told CNews television.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked and 78 teaching staff had been injured in the demonstrations.

On Monday, BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille in northern France, tear gas being used ​in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being lit as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Union official 'appalled'

Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalized Lycee Vauquelin in Paris, said it had been attacked ⁠by a "very determined" group wearing hoods and masks who had tried to break through the entrance door and then lit a fire, forcing the school ⁠to be evacuated and classes suspended.
"It was very violent and happened very quickly," she said, adding that she did not believe the attackers were ⁠from the school.

Since ⁠last Monday, 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them teenagers, have been ​arrested and dozens injured. Teachers and members of the public have been attacked, while damage to property is estimated in the millions of euros.
Bregeon said the ​government would fast-track a bill on Oct. 27 ⁠to make youngsters found to have damaged property, or their parents, financially liable.
Security officials fear that Tuesday's organized protests in central Paris in particular could bring further violence amid concerns that far-left and anarchist groups could try to take them over.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT labor union, told TF1 television on Monday that her members would attend Tuesday's demonstrations to protect the students.
"We've been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the ⁠government has organized," she said.
